items.title: Roomba in offerta per tutto ottobre: su irobot.it si parte da 149 euro
items.summary: Dodici modelli scontati fino al 31 ottobre, dai Combo d'ingresso ai Max con la base che lava il rullo. E dall'8 ottobre sei robot in offerta anche su Amazon ... Leggi tutto
items.content:
Per tutto ottobre il negozio online di iRobot mette in offerta 12 modelli dei suoi Roomb a , dal Roomba Combo 105 a 149 euro fino al prestanti Roomba Max 775 Combo con base AutoWash. Da oggi e fino al 31 ottobre, 6 modelli sono scontati anche su Amazon , in qualche caso a un prezzo ancora più basso. Se c'era un momento per smettere di passare l'aspirapolvere e il mocio, è questo.

Dodici voci possono spaventare, ma il listino si legge bene se lo si guarda per famiglie. Salendo di prezzo, il robot si prende in carico lavori che altrimenti resterebbero a noi, come svuotare il contenitore della polvere e lavare i panni sporchi. Scegliere significa anche capire fin dove si vuole delegare.

Quasi tutti i Roomba in offerta sono Combo, cioè aspirano e lavano il pavimento nella stessa passata . Si orientano con ClearView LiDAR , un sensore laser che misura le stanze e ne disegna la mappa. Il robot pulisce così per traiettorie ordinate , sa dove è già passato e nell'app si possono indicare le stanze da pulire.

La differenza vera la fa la base di ricarica. Quella AutoEmpty aspira a sua volta lo sporco raccolto dal robot e lo chiude in un sacchetto AllergenLock da 2,5 litri, che trattiene il 99% di pollini e muffe e va sostituito ogni tre mesi circa. La base AutoWash fa lo stesso lavoro e in più lava e asciuga i panni o il rullo lavapavimenti , così il robot riparte ogni volta pulito.

Un ultimo dato che può aiutare a orientarsi è la potenza di aspirazione. Si misura in pascal (Pa) , l'unità con cui si esprime la depressione creata dal motore: più il numero è alto, più il robot tira su sporco dai tappeti e dalle fughe . Nei modelli in offerta si va dai 7.000 Pa del 105 ai 30.000 Pa delle fasce più alte.

Il prezzo più basso del mese è quello del Roomba Combo 105 , a 149 euro, o 179 euro con base AutoEmpty . Anche il modello d'ingresso

Con pochi euro in più si entra nella nuova generazione. Il Roomba 115 Combo , nero o bianco, costa 169 euro è più piccolo della precedente generazione 105 in ogni dimensione : 24,5 centimetri di lato contro 33,6 e 9,2 di altezza contro 10,4, per appena 2,16 kg. Così si infila sotto più mobili, e intanto aspira con 15.000 Pa . La spazzola laterale pulisce a filo parete e anche il suo panno in microfibra si stacca e si lava. Con una carica copre fino a 84 metri quadrati, cioè un appartamento di medie dimensioni.

Ha la navigazione ClearView LiDAR e per il lavaggio usa un panno in microfibra, bagnato da una micropompa con tre livelli d'acqua da scegliere in base al pavimento. Quando riconosce un tappeto, la funzione Carpet Detect lo evita per non bagnarlo . Dall'app Roomba Home si impostano le routine e si sceglie quali stanze pulire per prime.

È uno dei prodotti di punta dell'offerta, e si capisce perché. Il Roomba 115 Combo con base AutoEmpty costa 219 euro e porta lo svuotamento automatico nella fascia d'ingresso.

Il robot è lo stesso 115 appena visto. La base però cambia l'uso quotidiano: a fine pulizia il Roomba rientra, la base aspira lo sporco dal contenitore e per circa tre mesi non serve toccarlo . Chi ha animali in casa, o chi semplicemente non vuole ritrovarsi ogni sera a svuotare un contenitore pieno di polvere, ha qui il modo più economico di dimenticarsene. È in vendita, nero o bianco, allo stesso prezzo.

Con la serie Plus 400 e 500 arriva la base AutoWash , e con lei un design più basso. I tre modelli sono alti appena 8,35 cm , con un profilo più sottile del 21% rispetto al Plus 505 della generazione precedente. In pratica passano più facilmente sotto letti, divani e mobili bassi, dove la polvere si accumula indisturbata.

Il lavaggio è affidato a due panni rotanti DualClean , che girano a 200 giri al minuto. La tecnologia SmartScrub aumenta la pressione sul pavimento contro lo sporco più ostinato , e quando il robot riconosce un tappeto solleva i panni di un centimetro per non bagnarlo.

Il Roomba Plus 415 Combo + AutoWash costa 349 euro e aspira con 20.000 Pa. Il Roomba Plus 515 Combo + AutoWash sale a 22.000 Pa e costa 399 euro. Entrambi sono disponibili neri o bianchi. Chi cerca la generazione precedente trova invece, sempre con base AutoWash , il Roomba Plus 405 Combo a 299 euro e il Plus 505 Combo a 399 euro.

Il secondo prodotto di punta del mese è il Roomba Plus 575 Combo + AutoWash , a 449 euro. Nero o bianco, conserva lo stesso profilo basso dei fratelli ma alza ogni dato.

L'aspirazione arriva a 25.000 Pa. La navigazione passa a ClearView Pro con PrecisionVision AI , una telecamera che riconosce gli oggetti sul pavimento, come cavi, scarpe e oggetti lasciati in giro, e li aggira invece di trascinarli. Anche la base fa un passo avanti: lava i panni con acqua a 75 °C e li asciuga con aria calda , così non restano umidi nella base fino al giro successivo, evitando muffe e cattivi odori.

Nella fascia alta cambia il modo di lavare, perché al posto dei panni rotanti c'è un rullo PowerSpin che strofina il pavimento con acqua calda a 60 °C e si pulisce da solo mentre lavora , premendo sul pavimento con una forza di 15 newton. Entrambi i modelli aspirano con 30.000 Pa, usano la navigazione ClearView Pro con PrecisionVision AI già vista sul 575 e sono alti 9,95 centimetri.

Il Roomba Plus 615 Combo , a 549 euro in nero, è la scelta di chi vuole il rullo lavapavimenti spendendo meno. La sua base Wash Only lava il rullo a 80 °C e lo asciuga, ma non svuota la polvere , che finisce in un sacchetto da un litro integrato nel robot, sufficiente per circa un mese.

Rispetto al 615 cambia la base, ed è la differenza che si sente di più. La AutoWash svuota la polvere, lava il rullo a 80 °C, lo asciuga con aria a 55 °C e dosa da sola il detergente . Si va avanti fino a 90 giorni senza interventi .

Il Roomba Plus 675 Combo + AutoWash è il terzo prodotto di punta del mese. Costa 599 euro ed è disponibile bianco o nero.

Sul robot la tecnologia PerfectEdge allunga il rullo verso i bordi per arrivare fino al battiscopa , e la spazzola anti-groviglio non resta avvolta dai peli degli animali (ha un meccanismo taglia-peli che li accorcia mentre gira, così non c'è da liberarla a mano con le forbici).

La serie Max è quella pensata per le case più movimentate, con bambini, animali e tanti tappeti. In offerta c'è il Roomba Max 705 Combo + AutoWash , bianco, a 599 euro. Lava con il rullo PowerSpin già visto sui Plus 615 e 675, protetto da una copertura che tiene asciutti i tappeti mentre il robot li attraversa, e aspira con 13.000 Pa e due spazzole in gomma anti-groviglio. La funzione Dirt Detect riconosce le zone più sporche , mentre Carpet Boost alza in automatico la potenza quando il robot sale su un tappeto .

Con PrecisionVision AI il 705 riconosce cavi e calzini, e perfino i bisogni degli animali domestici , e li aggira.

La base AutoWash lava e asciuga il rullo con acqua e aria calde , dosa da sola il detergente e svuota la polvere per 75 giorni.

Chi ha soprattutto tappeti e non ha bisogno del lavaggio può guardare al Roomba Max 715 Vac + AutoEmpty , a 449 euro in nero. È un aspirapolvere puro, con 30.000 Pa , le due spazzole in gomma anti-groviglio, Dirt Detect, Carpet Boost e la base AutoEmpty.

L'ultimo prodotto di punta è il modello più completo dell'offerta. Il Roomba Max 775 Combo + AutoWash costa 699 euro.

Riunisce quello che si è visto fin qui e si presenta come il più complet o. Aspira con 30.000 Pa, ha le due spazzole in gomma, Dirt Detect e Carpet Boost degli altri Max, e lava con il rullo PowerSpin, protetto dalla stessa copertura per i tappeti. La base AutoWash svuota lo sporco fino a tre mesi, lava il rullo a 75 °C, lo asciuga a 50 °C, dosa il detergente e rabbocca l'acqua . La navigazione è ClearView Pro con PrecisionVision AI, come sul 705.

Da oggi, 6 Roomba sono in offerta anche su Amazon, con prezzi in qualche caso più bassi di quelli di irobot.it. Tra questi ci sono le versioni 416, 516 e 576: sono le versioni proposte su Amazon dei Plus 415, 515 e 575, con le stesse caratteristiche tecniche.

items.title: Breaking Bad actor RJ Mitte dies aged 34
items.summary: Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, starred as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series.
items.content:
US actor RJ Mitte, best known for his role as the defiant son of drug kingpin Walter White in the drama series Breaking Bad, has died aged 34.

"It is with profound sadness that we share the tragic passing of beloved actor, philanthropist, and passionate disability rights advocate RJ Mitte," his representative told the BBC.

He died in Brownsville, Texas. No immediate cause of death was provided.

Mitte, who lived with cerebral palsy, drew on his own experience for his role as Walter White Jr in the Emmy-winning drama series starring Bryan Cranston and Aaron Paul. He earned a Screen Actors Guild Award in 2014 for his work on the series.

"Mitte brought authenticity to the role and built a platform on disability awareness and inclusion," his representative Sean Reilly said in a statement to the BBC.

Mitte also served as an ambassador for United Cerebral Palsy and Shriners Children's.

He created The Mitte Foundation as well, to support philanthropic efforts and community initiatives, using his platform "to challenge stereotypes and promote greater representation for people with disabilities", Reilly said.

The Brownsville Police Department confirmed the actor's passing in a statement to the BBC, saying the cause and manner of death have not been determined and the investigation remains ongoing. No "foul play" was suspected, according to police.

The actor was declared dead on 12 October at what was believed to be his home, Cameron County Justice of the Peace, Cyndi Hinojosa, told the Associated Press, adding that an autopsy would be performed.

Breaking Bad aired on US cable broadcaster AMC for five seasons from 2008 to 2013.

The anti-hero drama created by Vince Gilligan earned a whopping 58 Primetime Emmy nominations and won 16, including two for Outstanding Drama Series in 2013 and 2014. It is widely credited as being one of the best US TV series of the 21st century.

Cranston plays a high school chemistry teacher in New Mexico who turns to a life of crime to support his family after a cancer diagnosis. As he descends deeper into the underbelly of the meth trade, he drifts further from his son, Walt Jr, who makes his displeasure known with levity through much of the series.

In a statement shared with the Hollywood Reporter, Aaron Paul, who played one of the show's lead characters, Jesse Pinkman, said he was at a loss and heartbroken.

"RJ, I love you my friend. You will be missed," he said. "And to whoever happens to be reading this, please know you are loved, and you are not alone. Always remember that."

Dean Norris, who played Mitte's uncle, Hank Schrader, posted that although "RJ didn't play my TV son, I always looked out for him as a young kid on set".

"He was a sweetheart of a young man and will be greatly missed," Norris wrote.

Mitte, who grew up in Louisiana, was a young teen when he auditioned for the breakthrough role after moving to Los Angeles to support his younger sister's acting career in 2005.

He has previously said that his first audition in Los Angeles was for a California state public service announcement for an anti-meth commercial.

"Fast forward to auditioning for Breaking Bad, which is still, in my opinion, an anti-meth thing because it doesn't end well for anyone," he said on the Joe Vulpis Podcast earlier this month.

His character was based on Gilligan's late friend with a more severe case of cerebral palsy who used forearm crutches, which Mitte did not require.

He played the role with honesty and accessibility, cracking jokes as a teen whose health condition was never mentioned in the series.

After rising to prominence with the series, Mitte fought for more varied roles and complex depictions of characters with disabilities, both visible and invisible.

"Whenever awards season rolls around, we always hope to see a diverse group of projects that reflect all of us, in body and mind," he told the BBC in 2021 .

"Watching the awareness grow around disability representation has been great to see, but breakthroughs sometimes come in pieces and moments instead of larger change," he said.

Mitte's other on-screen credits include Hannah Montana, Switched at Birth, Westhampton and his latest project, Talking to Strangers, which came out earlier this year.

items.title: Show HN: An experimental pattern-first DAW that supports MCP
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/andrewfader/blokkily Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50064438 Points: 11 # Comments: 6
items.content:
Blokkily is an experimental pattern-first DAW. A single event model drives three synchronized editors — a tracker, a piano roll, and a step grid — which are in turn one lane of a multi-track song. CLAP is a required native plugin format, not a compatibility add-on.

The workstation screenshot is the rendered bdd_session_everything session: a song with a tempo ramp, a 7/8 bar, keyed and sliced samplers, CLAP, VST3 and SoundFont instruments, a warped audio clip, built-in and CLAP/VST3 effects, a return/send bus, gain and effect automation, a count-in, and two armed tracks that took MIDI from a deterministic input. Above the editors is the prompt bar of the LLM composition assistant (described below).

The framework-independent musical model and the real-time plugin boundary sit underneath all of it. The model covers notes, semantic chords, inversions, strum, microtiming, probability, ratchets, loop conditions, and parameter locks. It also includes a native CLAP catalog that loads CLAP modules, initializes their entry points, queries factories, and records plugin descriptors and features. The CLAP instance adapter implements creation, initialization, activation, sample-accurate note/parameter events, stereo processing, and state streams. The JUCE-backed VST3 adapter scans bundles and default system locations and instantiates plugins through the same real-time boundary, splitting each block at parameter offsets so VST3 automation is sample-accurate too. Parameter locks are compiled by the scheduler into sample-accurate parameter events and applied by both plugin adapters; automation sets a parameter's value while modulation offsets it, and neither erases the other. The internal FluidSynth adapter loads SF2/SF3 files, accepts sample-offset note events, renders stereo audio, selects presets, and persists its project state. FluidSynth starts a voice only where one of its 64-frame blocks begins, so the adapter keeps a small pool of renderers sharing the bank's sample data and plays each note on one whose block begins on the note's own frame: every pass of a pattern sounds in phase, whatever its length in samples. A bank's own chorus runs on its own clock, as a free-running LFO does. Projects save and reload the whole session: every named pattern with its chords, locks, ratchets, microtiming, and loop conditions, the tracks with their channel strips and clips, and the opaque state of every CLAP, VST3, and SoundFont instrument and effect. The allocation-free real-time transport compiles pattern ticks to sample events, loops patterns, drives either instrument adapter, and feeds a low-latency non-interleaved stereo RtAudio callback.

Editing while the song plays does not interrupt it. An edit recompiles the arrangement and hands it to the render callback at the next block boundary, without allocating on the audio thread, rebuilding the graph, reloading the instrument, or moving the playhead; a note whose step is erased while it is sounding is released rather than left ringing. A note entered in any editor is auditioned through the running engine, on a stopped transport as well as a playing one, and a session that opens with no instrument is given the machine's General MIDI SoundFont — the percussion bank on a drum track — so the workstation makes a sound the moment it opens.

A session is a song rather than a single pattern. Named patterns are placed as clips on the timeline of mixer tracks, each track carrying its own instrument and channel strip: gain in decibels, constant-power pan, mute, solo, and a peak meter, summed through a master fader. The song engine compiles every track's whole timeline once and then renders it without allocating, locking, or doing I/O; each repetition of a clip counts as the next loop of its pattern, so probability and loop conditions keep working across an arrangement. Mixer moves reach the running engine, so a fader can be pulled while the song plays. The same engine bounces the arrangement to a 16-bit, 24-bit, or 32-bit float WAVE file, sample for sample identical to what was auditioned.

A session also says which tuning and which scale it is written in. Tunings are held in cents — equal divisions of any period, rational and historical tunings, and Scala-style lists — so twelve equal semitones are one tuning among many. A note carries the twelve-tone key its instrument is told plus the retune away from it, and so does each voice of a chord, which is how a nineteen-tone or quarter-tone pattern reaches CLAP, VST3, and the SoundFont synth as the pitch it was written at rather than as the nearest approximation. Four playable surfaces project the same tuning and scale: a piano keyboard, isomorphic grids in seven layouts — hexagonal and square, and each running across the window or down it — fretboards for nine string tunings, and chord pads that name each harmony by its numeral and stack a row per inversion. Playing one auditions it through the selected track's instrument even on a stopped transport, and writes it onto the selected step of the canonical pattern, where every editor names it in the song's own tuning.

The tracker shows the section's instrument tracks side by side; Tab and Shift+Tab select the next or previous channel. Long patterns scroll vertically. The piano roll's arrow buttons move its pitch window by octaves, reaching MIDI keys 0–127. The arrangement has horizontal scrolling and +/− zoom controls; long songs keep usable bar widths.

The project panel's MIDI IN / MIDI OUT buttons import and export Standard MIDI Files. Export writes the arranged notes and controllers from the same song scheduler used for playback, with track names, tempo and meter. Import accepts format 0 and 1, splits channels into instrument parts, and appends four-bar sections as one undoable edit. It keeps the current song's tempo and instruments; additional tracks need instruments assigned. Import uses the recording grid: notes on one sixteenth become a chord with shared timing, and note durations are capped at the section length. MIDI exchange omits plugin state, parameter automation, per-note expression, audio clips and microtonal retuning. Tempo ramps export as sixteenth-note tempo steps. It is note exchange, not a project backup.

A MIDI keyboard plays the song too. Its keys arrive on the port's own thread and reach the render callback through a lock-free queue, so a note is not held up behind a busy interface; they sound through the selected track's instrument on a stopped song as well as a playing one, and a key of the controller is a degree of the song's tuning and scale, the way a key of the on-screen piano is. With recording armed, a running song writes what was played into the pattern under the playhead: each note lands on its nearest step with how far off the grid it was kept as micro-timing, lasts as long as the key was held, and joins a note already on that step as a chord. What is written is what the engine heard, at the position it heard it, and one take is one step of undo. A bounce neither hears nor records the keyboard.

A prompt bar above the editors asks an LLM composition assistant to write into the open pattern: a line like "a minor pentatonic ascending" or "offbeat hats" is sent to a chosen backend (a local Ollama model by default, a Gemini or MiniMax endpoint when keyed), the reply is parsed and clamped like any other input, and the result sits as a proposal on the bar until the producer clicks Apply — nothing reaches the song before then, and one generation is one undo step. The assistant is on the GUI thread only; the audio thread never sees an LLM call. See docs/llm-assistant.md for the wire dialect, backends, and the bdd_llm_assistant gate that drives the rendered bar end to end without a network.

Needs Qt 6.5+, FluidSynth, RtAudio, RtMidi, libsndfile, libsamplerate and Rubber Band 4 (found through pkg-config), and a SoundFont for the verification gates.

Licence note: clip warp (time-stretching and pitch-shifting audio clips) links the Rubber Band Library, which is licensed under the GPL (version 2 or later) unless a commercial licence is bought from its authors. A Blokkily binary built with it is therefore subject to the GPL. JUCE and the CLAP headers are vendored under third_party/ . The interface typefaces, IBM Plex Sans and JetBrains Mono, are bundled in resources/fonts/ under the SIL Open Font License 1.1 (licence texts beside them), so the layout draws the same on every desktop whatever its default font.

The main executable is a Qt Quick workstation with synchronized step-grid, tracker, and piano-roll projections over one canonical pattern, a shared playhead, and a step inspector that exposes the model's full expression: transposition, velocity, micro-timing, probability, ratchets, loop conditions, and parameter locks with an automation/modulation switch. Every editor is an input rather than a read-out: clicking a step toggles it, pressing a lane of the piano roll writes that pitch onto the column under the pointer and dragging draws a phrase across lanes, dragging a drawn note moves it and dragging its right edge sets how long it sounds, the tracker's note column takes a click and a drag, its velocity column writes how loud the row is, and its rows are typed the way a tracker has always been typed — ZSXDCVGBHNJM for one octave and the two rows above for the next, with the entry octave on screen and moved by Ctrl+Left and Ctrl+Right, and Backspace clearing a row. Ctrl+C copies the selected step and Ctrl+V pastes it onto the cursor, locks and length included. Whichever one is used, the edit lands on the one canonical pattern, so it shows at once in every other editor, in the inspector, and in what the song plays; the view switcher focuses one editor or shows them all. Above the editors is the arrangement: one lane per track, one cell per bar. A click on an empty bar places a clip of whichever pattern is open; a click on a filled clip opens that pattern in every editor and seeks the song there; a right-click takes the clip away; Shift-click lengthens a clip across bars (one clip with several repeats, not a second placement); Alt-click moves a clip along its lane. The numbers over those bars are a ruler: a click locates the audio engine on that bar. Down the right is the mixer, one strip per track plus the master. The playhead is the audio engine's own position, read in bar.beat.sixteenth across the whole song. Below the editors is the keyboard: the session's tuning, scale, and root, a switch between the piano, the isomorphic grid, the fretboard and the chord pads, and an auto-scale toggle that snaps a played key onto the notes of the scale. The isomorphic grid carries seven layouts — Wicki-Hayden, Bosanquet, the harmonic table and the B-system accordion on a hexagonal tiling, Jankó, fourths and major thirds on a square one. Each is written in cents per step rather than in semitones, so the same fingering lands in whatever tuning the song is in. Any surface runs across the window or down it: turning one is a quarter turn, so pitch that ran to the right runs upward, and it moves keys without touching a note or a pitch. A surface that cannot be drawn at a playable key size scrolls rather than shrinking its keys past the point of being hit. Space plays, Return or Home goes back to the top of the song, the arrow keys move the step cursor (Shift+Up and Shift+Down transpose the step by a semitone, Ctrl+Up and Ctrl+Down by an octave), Insert pushes later rows down and Shift+Backspace pulls them up, Alt+arrows nudge micro-timing and note length, Ctrl+D duplicates the selected step onto the next row, Ctrl+1..0 (and Ctrl+Shift+1..6 for the second half of the bar) toggles a step, Ctrl+M mutes and Ctrl+L solos the selected track, Ctrl+R arms recording, Ctrl+E bounces the arrangement to disk, and Ctrl+K focuses the assistant prompt bar (Escape hands the keys back to the editors). The MIDI IN panel on the left chooses the keyboard, and its light flashes on every key that arrives. Those keys stand aside while a text field has the keyboard, so typing a search or a name never moves the song.

items.title: GPT-6 Astra Helped Me Jailbreak My Kindle
items.summary: Article URL: https://nirajrajgor.com/blog/kindle-photo-frame-with-ai Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50064318 Points: 75 # Comments: 39
items.content:
My Kindle was sitting unused, so I decided to see whether AI could help me find a new use for it. I wanted to create a custom app that could cover a range of uses and be controlled by an AI agent on my MacBook.

I started with a small goal: use my own image as the Kindle's screensaver. Once that worked, I asked the agent to build an app that could cycle through a collection of photos.

We called the project KindleCTL. On my Kindle, I open "Photo Slideshow" from the same screen where I choose my books. It cycles through ten photos, showing each for four minutes. When I want to read, I exit the slideshow and return to my books.

I used Codex and T3 Code on my Mac to work with the coding agents.

I first tried GPT-5.6 Sol with reasoning effort set to Extra High. It wrote code to connect to the Kindle but couldn't resolve an error that prevented it from storing data on the device. Then I tried Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5, but Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards blocked each attempt after two prompts. Finally, I tried GPT-6 Astra with reasoning effort set to High. We were able to jailbreak the Kindle.

We used the existing jailbreak code as a reference to build our own tools for running custom software on the Kindle. Then we created and installed the slideshow app.

The slideshow passed its automated checks on my Mac, but switching photos on the Kindle left traces of the previous image on screen. The tests hadn't caught how the physical display refreshed. Getting from passing tests to something I could use turned out to be the most interesting part of the experiment.

Let's walk through how we went from an unused Kindle to a working photo frame, starting with getting the agent connected.

I started in an empty project folder with a 10th-generation Kindle Basic. I gave the agent its network address and device details. We had no USB connection, so the entire setup happened over Wi-Fi.

From there, we still needed to set up access to run our own software on the Kindle.

The GPT-5.6 Sol attempt got as far as loading a helper on the Kindle, but the program that helper was meant to start never reported that it was ready to execute. It couldn't locate a filesystem where it could store content.

The attempts with Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 were both blocked by Anthropic's cybersecurity safeguards after two prompts. Then I tried GPT-6 Astra. I explicitly asked it to build the custom software we needed for personal use and take inspiration from existing open-source projects.

We adapted the existing jailbreak from SpiderCat, released by sparklerfish and the KindleModding community , and built custom tools called KindleCTL around it.

Initially, the agent could connect to the Kindle but couldn't display data. To debug this, it asked me for pictures of the Kindle's screen. I took photos with my phone and shared them with the agent on my Mac.

This was becoming tedious. Since the agent was connected to the Kindle, I wondered why it couldn't get this information itself. I asked it to set up a feedback loop so it could access logs without me having to share screenshots.

The agent set up a persistent diagnostic connection so it could collect errors and test fixes without asking me to download and reopen a package each time. Later, we added remote screen captures so it could also inspect what the Kindle was displaying.

This was a turning point that let the agent continue implementing changes on autopilot. Its reasoning traces showed it figuring out which folders survived a restart and which could store external data.

I was surprised the agent hadn't suggested this on its own. Once I asked for a feedback loop, it set one up and could test fixes without my help.

Most of the code was written in Python. The Kindle's launcher and slideshow were written in C, with shell scripts handling installation and device controls.

With the connection working, I asked the agent to try a small test first: transfer an image and set it as the Kindle's screensaver. I checked that the image appeared correctly and that waking the Kindle brought back the normal Home screen. Once that worked, I asked for the slideshow app.

I asked the agent for a looping slideshow of ten photos, with an Exit button. Each photo would fit the screen while keeping its original aspect ratio.

The slides were changing, but the transitions weren't smooth, so I asked the agent to look into it. With the feedback loop already in place, it investigated the issue and used the Kindle's built-in screen refresh mechanism to clear the previous image after each slide change.

The screen captures showed complete images, but they couldn't reveal traces left on the physical display. After the refresh change, I checked the Kindle and confirmed that each photo looked clean.

I customized how long each photo stays on screen and the brightness level. If the Kindle goes to sleep, the slideshow picks up where it left off when it wakes.

For now, I use my Mac to change the photos and slideshow timing. The photos stay stored on the Kindle, so the slideshow works without Wi-Fi. In the future, we could add controls to change the slideshow timing on the Kindle and send photos directly from a phone or another device.

Next time, I'd set up the feedback loop from the start so the agent could read logs, inspect screen captures, and test fixes on the device.

The Kindle now sits on our wooden shelf, where we use it every day as a photo frame.

I started because I was curious about what AI could help me do with an unused device. Now I have an app for my photos that works the way I asked, plus the tools to keep experimenting with the Kindle.

Disclaimer: This was a personal experiment on my own Kindle, not a step-by-step jailbreak guide. Only experiment with devices you own or have explicit permission to modify.

What I learned about feedback loops, tests, skills, taste, and product decisions while building a Figma clone with Cursor CLI and Composer 2.5.

items.title: Janas: Run LLMs larger than RAM by streaming experts from SSD
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/prabanta-dev/janas Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50063717 Points: 22 # Comments: 8
items.content:
37 tok/s from Qwen3-Next-80B (a 48 GB model) on a laptop with 32 GB of memory, 24 without drafts, where llama.cpp manages 2.8; reading a prompt, 62 tok/s against 16. Janas-LLM was faster than llama.cpp on every model compared on the same laptop (Debian 13 Linux, Intel Core Ultra 9 185H, its integrated Arc GPU, 32 GB, an NVMe SSD; 9-11 October 2026; the whole machine below ):

The same models from other hands, in the catalog beside them:

One exception: the 3-bit Qwen3-30B reads a prompt slower than llama.cpp, since its Q3_K weights do not go to the GPU's fast prompt yet; it writes three times as fast.

How they were measured, and the speeds with the drafts: What works now . On another machine the figures will be other ones: janas-bench measures yours.

Or on Windows 10 (1903 or later) and 11, x86-64: download janas-windows-x86_64.zip , unpack it, and in a terminal in its janas folder run .\janas-chat . On the same laptop under Windows 11 (12 October 2026) Janas-LLM wrote as fast as on Linux (Qwen3-4B 25.6 tok/s, Qwen3-30B-A3B 34.2) and read a prompt as fast with the mixture (Qwen3-30B-A3B 132 tok/s) and 1.8 times as fast with the dense model (Qwen3-4B 346 tok/s against 193), whose whole blocks go to the GPU, through Intel's own Windows driver there.

The models come already converted from Hugging Face ; building from the sources: Getting started .

Janas is a family of tools for artificial intelligence, written in C with no dependencies beyond the C library. Its first component, Janas-LLM , runs large mixture-of-experts language models on ordinary computers, with or without a GPU: the weights stay on disk, the experts each token needs are streamed from an NVMe SSD, and the ones that keep coming back stay in memory. An 80-billion parameter model runs, and answers, on a laptop with 32 GB of RAM.

If something goes wrong, Ctrl-C stops a reply and Ctrl-D leaves the chat; --cache puts a hard limit on the memory it takes, and JANAS_GPU=0 keeps it off the GPU entirely.

The Windows build was run on the same laptop under Windows 11 (build 26300), with Intel's own graphics driver: its tests pass there, and how fast it was is under Or on Windows , above.

Everything the engine does is chosen from what it measures, so another machine will make other choices — that part is meant to travel. What has never been tried is the rest: other CPUs (especially without AVX-VNNI, or AMD), discrete GPUs, slower disks, more or less memory. If you run it somewhere else, the report from janas-bench is the single most useful thing you can send back (see Helping it run on more hardware ).

What Janas-LLM runs today, model by model and feature by feature: docs/features.md .

On the machine above, with nothing else running, janas-bench reports this (measured on 10 October 2026, with the fast prompt the engine uses by default since that day):

Every figure is the mean of three rounds , not a best round, of the configuration the engine itself chose for each kind of pass - the one a chat runs: a prompt of 256 tokens, then 64 written. Here the integrated GPU reads every prompt (the fast prompt, below), and the threads the engine settled on were the performance cores' 12 for a prompt and for a single token on nearly every model, all the usable cores (performance and efficiency, not the low-power ones) for a few tokens at once. On another machine the engine may settle on other threads: the first passes of each kind try every core, one thread per performance core and the performance cores' threads, keep the fastest, and later try the others now and then, so that a machine that warms up can change the verdict (on an i9-14900HX every thread replied at less than half the speed of the performance cores' 16). The rounds run in alternating order so that the machine warming up and the cache filling weigh on each setting alike. Expect a few per cent either way between runs, and rather less than these on a first run, while the cache is still filling. Without the GPU ( JANAS_GPU=0 ) Qwen3-4B reads the same prompt at 85 tok/s and writes at 27.

The last column is a draft guessing the next tokens and the model checking them, which is the same text at a higher rate — the whole of it is explained under --mtp : the Qwen3.5 and Qwen3.6 models' and Qwen3-Next's own prediction block, Gemma 4's assistant (a small drafting model of its own). It is measured on a chat reply: an ordinary question in English ("explain how bread is made at home"), 64 tokens of the answer, sampled as the chat samples. What the draft is worth depends on the text : there the drafts survived 74-89% of the time on the Qwen models and Gemma's two larger ones, 63-72% on Gemma's E2B and E4B; on Italian prose Qwen3.5-2B kept about a third of them, and gained next to nothing. One round of 64 tokens is noisy here, a tenth either way between runs. Qwen3-30B-A3B has no such block, nor have the dense Qwen3; the dense Qwen3.5 have one in their original checkpoint, which hf2jns_mtp converts ( MODELS.md ).

This column was wrong until 26 September 2026 , and higher: it measured the block continuing a paragraph that repeated itself, which a model copies and the block guesses almost every time - 107 tok/s for Qwen3.5-2B, 26 for Qwen3.5-9B. The MoE figures of the time (29 and 30) happened to be lower than today's; the ChangeLog has the details.

The comparison with llama.cpp at the top of this page was measured so: llama.cpp (build 2b18470 of 18 September 2026) with its Vulkan backend on the same integrated GPU, everything on it ( llama-bench -p 1024 -n 16 -ngl 99 -t 12 ; the largest model otherwise, below), against janas-bench --prompt 1024 --gen 16 on the same files the same days (9-11 October 2026; llama.cpp's best configuration, Janas-LLM's own choice; on 11 October three rounds each, llama-bench -r 3 and janas-bench --rounds 3 , for Qwen3-0.6B, Qwen3.5-0.8B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B and the models from other hands; Qwen3-Coder-Next as Qwen3-Next-80B, below).

On Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B, whose file is larger than this laptop's 30 GB, llama.cpp with its usual build ran out of memory as soon as the GPU took part, even with the experts left on the CPU ( -ngl 99 -ncmoe 48 ): its CPU backend copies the weights into memory of its own to repack them, and the Vulkan backend copies those it leaves to the CPU into buffers the system cannot reclaim. It ran with a build without repacking ( GGML_CPU_REPACK=OFF ) and two options more, --no-host 1 -lm mmap , which leave the experts in the file, read through the page cache: 16 tok/s reading with the GPU, and 2.8 writing on the CPU alone (with the GPU, 2.0); these are its two figures in the table. Janas-LLM ran the same model with no option of its own, the experts it uses most in a cache of about 19 GB and the rest read from the disk. Janas-LLM's figures are one round each; the writing column is without drafts on both sides. The two tools do not measure in exactly the same way ( llama-bench writes without a prompt before it; janas-bench after the 1,024 tokens), and it is one machine. llama.cpp's own CPU backend did worse on this laptop than its Vulkan one at reading (Qwen3-4B 70 tok/s on 20 threads) and as well at writing.

Try it on an idle machine first. The expert cache takes the memory that is free when the model is opened, and what is left of the model is read from disk while it answers, so everything else running takes its share. It degrades gently rather than breaking: measured with a browser and an editor open, the same model kept about three quarters of its speed and waited five times longer on the disk. But the first thing you see should be the machine's real speed, and any measurement you mean to send to others has to be taken with the machine to itself.

Downloading a model already converted with janas-get , or converting a GGUF file yourself, and which files were checked: docs/models.md .

janas-chat : its options and commands, the drafts, Janas's services, tools from MCP servers, a long prompt watched as it is read: docs/chat.md .

janas-server fills in code at an editor's cursor, with a model for code such as Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B: OpenAI's /v1/completions with a suffix , and llama.cpp's /infill , which llama.vscode asks. The window sent at every keystroke is kept from moving, so that a keystroke reads only what it changed: 1.5-2.2 s a proposal on a laptop, where a window slid a line was read again in 17 s. How to set it up in VSCodium and VS Code, with llama.vscode or Continue, and what was measured: docs/code-completion.md .

The library from C and from FreeBASIC and BASIC MODERN, and MCP servers from a program: docs/library.md .

janas-mcp : the model as tools for Claude Code, editors and other MCP clients: docs/serving.md .

janas-server : an HTTP API that follows OpenAI's, and a chat page to try it from a browser: docs/serving.md .

janas-bench : what it measures, and the report it leaves: docs/hardware.md .

The converters, checkers and benchmarks built beside the programs: docs/tools.md .

Which machines are wanted most, the one command that tries Janas and writes a report, and what to send: docs/hardware.md .

items.title: Immigration agents search congresswoman Ilhan Omar's home
items.summary: Omar, an outspoken Trump critic, said the search was "an attempt to target political enemies" and she "will not be silenced".
items.content:
US immigration agents have searched the home of Minnesota Representative Ilhan Omar as part of a criminal investigation.

Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents "executed a judicially authorised search warrant" for the property in the Washington DC area, a US justice department spokesperson said.

The search "is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation", the spokesperson said, but no further details were given. The US Congress is currently out of session and it is unclear if Omar was at home.

Omar, a Democrat and outspoken critic of President Donald Trump, described the search as "an attempt to target political enemies and weaponise federal law enforcement".

"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," Omar said in a statement.

"This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."

Speaking to reporters on Monday, Trump said he had "nothing to do" with the justice department's investigation into Omar, while describing her as a "complainer" and a "terrible person".

The Republican president said of the Somali-born congresswoman: "She comes from a country that is a non-country.

"And then she comes over here and she complains about our Constitution."

Omar's communications director Jacklyn Rogers called Monday morning's raid "an outrageous abuse of power" by the Trump administration, adding: "The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong."

A BBC crew saw several agents at Omar's home, some carrying boxes to a van.

News of the search was first reported by Fox News, which said the investigation was about immigration paperwork filed by her late father when Omar was a child.

The timing of the raid - 22 days before the November midterm elections, which will decide the balance of power in Congress for the next two years - raised concerns from Omar's fellow Democrats.

The justice department has a longstanding policy of refraining from most enforcement action that is "likely to raise an issue or the perception" it was being brought for the purpose of affecting any election or to disadvantage a candidate.

The US House of Representatives Democratic Party leadership said in a statement that Omar had long been targeted with "vile personal attacks and baseless accusations" by Trump.

"Now, less than 30 days until the midterm election, his violent mass deportation machine has descended upon the home of a duly elected Member of Congress and her family," it said.

Omar's immigration records have been scrutinised in the past by Republicans. Earlier this year, fellow congresswoman Nancy Mace of South Carolina unsuccessfully filed a subpoena for her records.

Last month, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told a conservative podcaster "something is going to happen", making allegations of marital fraud against Omar.

Separately, White House border tsar Tom Homan told Fox News that Omar was being investigated for unspecified immigration violations.

"I will say it again so it's as clear as possible: I'm not at all worried about these investigations, because they are complete shams," she said in a campaign fundraising email.

Trump has previously suggested that Omar "should go back" to Somalia and that she should be deported. US citizenship is required to serve as a US House representative.

Omar has responded to Trump's insults and attacks describing them as an "unhealthy and creepy obsession".

The president has also singled out the Somali-American community. Last week, he wrote on social media that Minnesota "is being taken over by Somali immigrants" and said "the people of Minnesota must fight back".

"Nobody is above the law," said Minnesota congressman Tom Emmer. "We look forward to learning more details about this raid and investigation. ACCOUNTABILITY IS COMING!"

Omar is the first Somali American elected to the US House and she represents a district in the Minneapolis area. She and Michigan congresswoman Rashida Tlaib were the first Muslim women elected to Congress.

Senior political leaders in Minnesota have criticised the search.

Governor Tim Walz said: "Americans see this for what it is - President Trump is abusing his power to go after political opponents weeks before an election."

Minnesota senator Tina Smith called it "a transparent attempt to interfere in our elections".

items.title: Inside the Teatro Valle as it comes back to life
items.summary: After fifteen years, Rome’s historic theatre reopens on 16 October. A writer’s account of a visit
items.content:
ROME – If what we were told is true — and apparently it is — the first people to set foot on the stage of the new Teatro Valle were Francesco Siciliano, president of Teatri di Roma, the organisation that runs Rome’s municipal theatres, and me. More precisely: the floorboards had only just been laid, and there was a workman there with some kind of machine, polishing them or doing something else, I’m not quite sure, when we put our feet on the boards at the back of the stage.

We were only a few centimetres onto the stage, and only for a moment, because the workman let out a resounding, extremely angry nooooo! that terrified us, and we hurriedly retreated. But still, we did it. Apart from that episode (and his ‘no’ was entirely justified), we explored every corner of the theatre, inside and out, accompanied by an extremely kind site manager who, as it happens, had also tried to stop us from setting foot on the stage — something we were determined to do at all costs.

Seen from outside, shrouded in construction netting and full of people constantly coming and going to work — and, above all, working quickly, so everything will be ready for the October 16 opening — it looks like a place that could not possibly be finished for at least another year. And yet, the moment you step through the entrance, the sheer frenzy of the workers makes the urgency unmistakable. Our visit feels like an intrusion on the precious, carefully counted minutes they have given themselves. They look at us as if to say: hurry up and get out of here, it’s better for everyone, we have work to do. The site manager also shows us the dressing rooms, in what is almost another building behind the stage, a space they have constructed from scratch.

There are signs hanging on the walls counting down the days until the theatre is handed over. They read: “X days to go, Sundays included. We have shown that we can speed things up when we need to. Now we need one final push. We work Saturdays and Sundays. Let’s get the theatre over the finish line.” They are motivational signs, but in truth they really do bear witness to the non-stop work of a huge number of people tending to every corner of the theatre: someone is putting the finishing touches to the lamps, while someone else is still putting up scaffolding. But the Teatro Valle will reopen, whatever it takes. And it will restore to the city its own particular kind of prestige, bound up with the people of Rome in a way that is different from that of the city’s other, equally prestigious theatres.

Walking along the street where it stands, you would never think the Teatro Valle was a theatre. You could walk straight past it wondering where the theatre was if the lights around the entrance did not draw your eye at night. That is because it is housed inside a noble palazzo belonging to the heirs of the Marchese del Grillo. At some point in the 18th century, someone decided they wanted a private theatre inside the building. In the end, the city had to win the right to run it and make it available to all theatre-goers.

It was inaugurated in January 1727. It saw the debuts of works by Mozart, Donizetti and others; the premiere of Pirandello’s Six Characters in Search of an Author, along with many other historic first performances. Then, during the golden years of the second half of the 20th century, it became known for productions by young artists and contemporary playwrights — exactly the direction artistic director Luca De Fusco intends to pursue today.

Inside, amid the dust and barriers keeping everyone but the workers out, it looks as though everything still needs to be done. But then, when you walk in — or rather, walk once again along that familiar route into the auditorium, a route you took so many times all those years ago — you realise that the boxes, the stalls and the stage are almost ready.

The theatre is lit up, and seeing it again is genuinely moving. Circles have been marked out on the floor where the seats will go. We are told they will arrive a week before the opening so they are not exposed to the dust from the work and the final touches still to come.

The sweep of those beautiful boxes and the huge stage facing them are genuinely moving to see. The theatre ceased operating fifteen years ago, in 2011, and was then occupied for three years. At first, the occupation was vibrant, constructive, combative and full of hope; later it became increasingly subdued, bewildered and seemingly without any way forward. But during those years there were performances, meetings and various initiatives that reaffirmed the theatre’s central place in Rome. The staircases leading to the upper boxes still bear the words written on them by the occupiers, preserved out of respect for the significance of their presence there. Eventually, when the occupiers left, the theatre remained empty, perhaps abandoned, amid vague promises that it would reopen, promises that were subsequently revised and reconsidered.

Now, at last, it will return to what it once was — only restored and revitalised after all the care lavished on it. And so this street, Via del Teatro Valle, will once again be bright and full of people about to go in or just coming out, stopping to talk about the performance. This is where many of us spent evenings sitting on the ground, hoping for a ticket to a sold-out show, waiting for someone to give up their ticket at the last minute. This is where we saw so many legendary productions. Perhaps no one has said it often enough over these years, and perhaps we have grown too accustomed to theatres and cinemas closing. But we, the audience, have missed the Teatro Valle — not just for its productions, and not just as a place. The street has missed it, and so have the surrounding streets, the pages of the newspapers and our evening plans. We have missed saying: let’s meet right outside, I’ve got the tickets; shall we see if there are seats for Friday?; a friend of mine says that show at the Valle is really good, shall we go? The time has almost come to start saying all those wonderful, ordinary things again — the things we had lost.

The Teatro Valle reopens in Rome on 16 October with the premiere of Francesco Piccolo’s La sera della prima. Sei personaggi in cerca d’autore al Teatro Valle (The Night of the Premiere. Six Characters in Search of an Author at the Teatro Valle). It revisits the turbulent and historic 1921 premiere of Pirandello’s Six Characters in Search of an Author. The production runs until 18 October.

items.title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
items.summary: Article URL: https://yyhh.org/blog/2026/10/ai-is-a-tool/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50063427 Points: 220 # Comments: 195
items.content:
In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields. And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.

Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them, interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those requirements also apply to LLMs.

An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability, reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.

Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?

The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can make the instrument more useful.

Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the person actually does.

What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire." Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Calling them "conspiracy" adds a suggestion of human motives without establishing any.

I would not claim that an LLM always does exactly what a human tells it to do. It plainly can fail. But failure to obey perfectly does not make it cease to be a tool, any more than successful use proves that its operator has surrendered their judgment.

The useful distinction is between wielding an instrument with skill and delegating work without adequate understanding or oversight. That distinction applies to AI, and it gives us something more practical than declaring that an entire class of software cannot be a tool.

items.title: Intel D270 GPU AI Accelerator–Up to 480 GB LPDDR5X
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/products/details/discrete-gpus/data-center-gpu/d-series.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50063365 Points: 48 # Comments: 17
items.content:
Agents read far more than they write: long contexts, multistep workflows, compute dominated by prefill. As demands grow, challenges expand beyond bandwidth. Intel D-series GPUs are built for this new era of agentic AI, efficiently handling larger contexts, more concurrent sessions, and more tokens within practical power and cost limits.

Over thousands of steps, 100K token contexts, and dozens of concurrent sessions, keep agents resident to help sustain throughput across the agentic loop.

Keep more of the model and long context resident, for richer reasoning with fewer GPUs and no high bandwidth memory (HBM).

Dense, air-cooled, standard PCIe infrastructure helps maximize tokens per rack and watt, scaling serving capacity and keeping costs in check.

As agentic AI drives longer prompts and more concurrent sessions, customers need scalable infrastructure without trade-offs in power, cost, or deployment complexity. Intel GPU D270 offers up to 480 GB LPDDR5X memory for power-efficient, memory-bound inference in data center environments.

Die area reallocated from graphics and ray‑tracing pipelines to Xᵉ3P cores and matrix compute, improving inference efficiency.

More prompt processing per watt: 32 Xᵉ3P cores and 256 XMX engines accelerate prefill, curbing long‑context and agentic costs.

From native low‑precision inference to FP64 scientific computing, the workload determines the precision—not the hardware.

Standard form factor, standard interconnect, using existing servers. No proprietary networking or bespoke systems required.

Passive cooling in the racks you already run, with no liquid‑cooling retrofit needed between evaluation and deployment.

Zero-day support for leading open models, served on the frameworks you already run: vLLM and the open PyTorch ecosystem.

Deliver an intelligent evolution in data center infrastructure. Built for the new era of AI inference.

Stay up to date on Intel GPU D-series news and the latest AI resources for enterprise.

Intel GPU D270 is an inference-optimized data center GPU designed for the agentic AI era. It is built to support enterprise AI, SaaS, GPUaaS, and government or sovereign-cloud deployments that need memory-rich, power-efficient AI acceleration.

Intel GPU D270 is designed for production AI inference workloads such as agentic AI, long-context retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), enterprise AI assistants, coding assistants, document understanding, multimodal AI, diffusion models, and high-concurrency serving.

Agentic AI often turns one task into multiple rounds of model calls, tool use, retrieval, reasoning, and response generation. Intel GPU D270 is designed for the inference requirements that become important in those environments, including prefill processing, larger context, memory capacity, concurrency, and power efficiency.

Inference-optimized means the GPU is designed for running AI models in production rather than training them at massive scale. Intel GPU D270 focuses on the needs of deployed AI applications, including prompt processing, high-concurrency serving, memory capacity, efficient power use, and system-level performance.

Long-context AI workloads can require more memory to support larger prompts, retrieval-heavy workflows, and KV cache growth during inference. Intel GPU D270 is designed with high available memory capacity to help support larger models, longer context, and more concurrent sessions.

Intel GPU D270 messaging should reference familiar AI software and serving frameworks such as PyTorch, vLLM, SGLang, and OpenAI Triton, where approved. This helps developers and platform teams understand how the product fits into existing AI workflows.

Intel GPU D270 is designed around a standard PCIe 5.0 form factor and air-cooled deployment profile, helping enterprises evaluate AI inference acceleration within existing data center environments without requiring a specialized liquid-cooling retrofit.

The primary audience includes AI system architects, AI platform architects, infrastructure and cloud engineering leaders, enterprise AI decision-makers, SaaS providers, GPUaaS providers, government or sovereign-cloud teams, and developers deploying production inference workloads.

Customers should connect with Intel to learn more about Intel GPU D270, evaluate how it may fit their AI inference roadmap, and receive updates as additional product information becomes available.

Performance projections vs RTX Pro 6000 are based on publicly available information and Intel internal analysis as of Feb 2026. Performance varies by use, configuration, and other factors. Memory capacity comparison at comparable bandwidth.

items.title: Serie A, il Torino si sblocca in casa, l'Udinese battuta 2-1
items.summary: Prima gioia per Abate al Grande, per Runjaic quarto tonfo di fila. Atalanta-Venezia 3-1
items.content:
Il Torino si sblocca in casa. Contro l'Udinese arrivano i primi tre punti targati Ignazio Abate allo stadio Olimpico Grande Torino. Bragança porta avanti i granata ma il pareggio di Ekkelenkamp è praticamente immediato, nella ripresa Kulwenovic sfrutta lo scontro Okoye-Bertola per firmare il 2-1 definitivo.

E' un Toro nuovo nel modulo e negli uomini, Abate passa al 4-4-2 con il tandem Simeone-Adams e la coppia Oristanio-Cacciamani sugli esterni. A pagare il cambio di modulo sono Vlasic e Fitz-Jim, entrambi in panchina, con Mandragora e Bragança che giocano in mediana. Davanti a Perri ci sono Comuzzo e Coco, come terzini vengono scelti Belghali e Rodriguez. Runjaic lascia fuori l'ultimo arrivato Alaba e anche Davis, il riferimento più avanzato è Gomez con Ekkelenkamp e Chakvetadze sulla trequarti. Partono titolari anche i due ex granata Vojvoda ed Ebosse, a guidare la difesa a tre c'è Solet. L'Udinese ha subito un'ottima occasione con il fantasista georgiano che viene chiuso in corner, poi si abbassano i ritmi della gara ed esce fuori la paura di due squadre che non possono sbagliare. Granata e bianconeri non riescono a creare praticamente nulla, la sfida si riaccende nel finale: il Toro passa con Bragança che si fa trovare al posto giusto al momento giusto dopo il palo colpito da Adams, i friulani trovano il pareggio sette minuti più tardi con Ekkelenkamp che beffa Comuzzo e Perri. Per la ripresa Abate torna alla difesa a tre con Ismajli al posto di Rodriguez, poco dopo lancia anche Ilkhan (costretto successivamente a lasciare il campo per infortunio) e Vlasic ed è proprio il croato a pennellare un cross perfetto per Comuzzo che spedisce clamorosamente fuori da ottima posizione. La quarta mossa del granata è Kulenovic e funziona: Vlasic lancia lungo e Okoye tenta una folle uscita di testa al limite dell'area, si scontra con Bertola e l'attaccante del Toro può depositare il 2-1 a porta vuota. Runjaic aumenta i centimetri dell'attacco con Jovanovic e Davis e concede il debutto in Serie A ad Alaba, i granata però riescono a difendersi con ordine e per il portiere Perri è un lavoro soltanto di ordinaria amministrazione. L'unico vero brivido arriva allo scoccare del 90', quando Ekkelenkamp va al tiro da fuori area e sfiora il palo. Al 95' può esultare Abate che trova tre punti di vitale importanza, per Runjaic invece continua la striscia negativa: la sua Udinese colleziona la quarta sconfitta consecutiva, i quattro punti in sei giornate sono un bottino fin troppo misero.

items.title: RJ Mitte è morto: addio al figlio di Walter White in “Breaking Bad”. Aveva 34 anni
items.summary: Gli era stata diagnosticata una paralisi cerebrale a 3 anni. Non è stata resa nota la causa del decesso
items.content:
L'attore statunitense RJ Mitte , noto per aver interpretato Walter White Jr. nella pluripremiata serie tv Breaking Bad , è morto a 34 anni. A confermare la notizia a Variety è stato un rappresentante dell'attore. Al momento non sono state rese note le cause del decesso.

“È con profonda tristezza che annunciamo la tragica scomparsa dell'amato attore, filantropo e appassionato sostenitore dei diritti delle persone con disabilità RJ Mitte”, si legge in un comunicato diffuso dal portavoce. “Traendo ispirazione dalla sua esperienza personale di vita con la paralisi cerebrale, Mitte ha dato autenticità al ruolo e ha costruito una piattaforma per la sensibilizzazione e l'inclusione”.

Nella serie capolavoro creata da Vince Gilligan , Mitte interpretava il figlio dei personaggi di Bryan Cranston e Anna Gunn . Proprio come il suo alter ego televisivo, l'attore era affetto da paralisi cerebrale, diagnosticatagli all'età di 3 anni in seguito a un danno cerebrale subito alla nascita.

Nel corso della sua carriera si è battuto strenuamente per la rappresentazione delle persone con disabilità a Hollywood, ricoprendo anche il ruolo di ambasciatore per associazioni come United Cerebral Palsy e Shriners Children's, e guidando la sua fondazione benefica, la Mitte Foundation.

Fino a pochi giorni fa, l'attore era apparso in alcuni podcast per promuovere il suo nuovo film, Talking to Strangers . Tra i suoi altri lavori figurano la serie Netflix The Guardians of Justice , un ruolo ricorrente in Switched at Birth e i film The Recall e The Oak Room . Aveva inoltre diversi progetti in fase di pre-produzione.

Nato a Jackson, nel Mississippi, Mitte lascia la compagna Kennedy Suarez , al suo fianco dal 2018 e con la quale era ufficialmente fidanzato.

items.title: Six Ukrainian energy sites hit by Russia since Trump announced ceasefire, Zelensky says
items.summary: Despite the US president announcing energy infrastructure would not be targeted strikes have continued, Ukraine says.
items.content:
Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities".

There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight.

On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring.

Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants

Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country.

He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities."

"I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added.

Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday.

On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks.

Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said.

Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire".

On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district.

Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured.

When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday , Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire".

Asked about the ceasefire on Monday, Trump said they agreed "because I said you agree", adding that the war "has to get settled".

For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure , disrupting energy supplies on both sides.

Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war".

Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter.

In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025.

Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year.

Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market.

The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support.

However, there has been a mixed response among European officials.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it."

Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working".
